subjects.displayTitle: Divine bounty: the gift that sustains existence
subjects.introduction: A fish may search for the very ocean that sustains it: this image gives a vivid entrance to a compilation in which existence itself is received, moment by moment, as divine bounty. Sunlight, flowing water, breath and spring rain express an outpouring that embraces all things while the source remains beyond the things it sustains. Several passages carefully distinguish emanation from the idea that God becomes divided among created beings; others move from the gift of physical existence to revelation, spiritual awakening and the growth of human capacities. Universal generosity and differing receptivity appear side by side, raising questions about effort, freedom and the cultivation of a responsive heart. The inquiry also has a practical consequence: those who receive an impartial bounty are called to offer kindness without exclusion or a hidden demand for reward. The connected subjects of the Holy Spirit, divine attributes within all things, and the soul as emanation open further paths into these questions. Supplied excerpts from Plotinus and Ibn ‘Arabi add distinct philosophical voices; the comparative readings below invite closer attention to Plotinus’s account of procession and the language of dependence and nearness in Acts. The aim is to read the similarities attentively while allowing each account—and each kind of source—to retain its own meaning.
subjects.arc: The sea in which we live → From the source, without becoming the source → Will, Word and the coming of existence → An unceasing gift → Revelation and the renewal of the world → Receiving what is freely given → Light within the human reality → Kinds of light and spiritual speech → Prayer, gratitude and return → Becoming a source of help → Further supplied voices

questions: What does it mean to depend on divine bounty at every moment, rather than only at the beginning of existence? How do the ocean, sunlight, breath and flowing water bring different aspects of that dependence into view?

How do the explanations of emanation distinguish a source from what proceeds from it? Where do the metaphors help, and where might taking them literally produce a meaning the passages themselves reject?

How can bounty be universal while its reception varies? What do the passages about capacity, effort and freedom suggest about a person’s responsibility for growth without making grace something merely earned?

How do the texts connect the sustaining of all existence with the appearance of the Manifestations and the renewal of spiritual life? What changes when the winter image is read together with the return of spring?
What does receiving without exclusion ask of the way we give to others? How do unconditional charity, useful action and love reflected from heart to heart connect this subject with everyday life?

What becomes clearer when Plotinus and Acts are read beside these selections, and which distinctions remain essential? Which connected subject—the Holy Spirit, divine attributes within all things, the soul as emanation, or emanation versus manifestation—would help deepen your next inquiry?

references.label: 1 · Plotinus, Enneads V.2 · Giving without depletion
references.note: Plotinus describes the One as the source of all things without identifying it with any one thing. His metaphor of overflow leads through Intellect and Soul; he cautions that this procession is not a movement through space. Compare the passage with the sun-and-rays analogy and the distinction between emanation and manifestation. How can a source give without becoming divided or diminished? The Neoplatonic sequence has its own structure and should not be treated as identical to the Baha’i account of God, Command and creation.
references.verified: Read both sections of Enneads V.2 in full on 2026-10-10 in the Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page translation hosted by Wabash College, including the explicit metaphor of overflow, the sequence of Intellect and Soul, and the rejection of spatial interpretation.

references.label: 2 · Acts 17:24–29 · Life received, nearness sought
references.note: This passage presents God as the giver of life and breath to all, brings the nations within a common origin, and joins the search for God to divine nearness. It also rejects reducing the divine to an image fashioned from material things. Read it beside the compilation’s language of continuing dependence and its call to treat every person with mercy. What might a shared source imply for human relationships? The Christian speech provides a comparison of dependence and nearness, rather than a technical account of emanation.
references.verified: Read Acts 17:24–29 in full in the King James Version on Bible Gateway on 2026-10-10, including life and breath, common human origin, the search for God, nearness and the rejection of manufactured images.
